title: DAPO Breakdown: How Four Mechanisms Lifted GRPO's Score on AIME 2024 from 30 to 50
subtitle: Reading an Engineering Post-Mortem of an Open-Source RL System from the Perspective of Structural Anatomy
markdown: > Breakdown Target: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale (arXiv:2503.14476 v2, submitted 2025-03-17, revised 2025-05-20), currently a preprint and not yet formally accepted at top conferences (dblp only lists it as arXiv). Authors from ByteDance Seed, Tsinghua University AIR, The University of Hong Kong, and SIA-Lab, with corresponding author Qiying Yu. This article does only one thing: analyze why the structure of this paper is good. All numbers and formulas come from the arXiv v2 main text and Appendix A, which can be cross-referenced with the original tables for verification. ## 1. Why It's Worth Breaking Down After R1, the community generally encountered three issues when reproducing GRPO: entropy collapse, reward signal noise, and training instability. The DeepSeek technical report did not explain how to handle these, but DAPO provided the solutions all at once. It lifted the AIME 2024 score from 30 (GRPO baseline) to 50 on Qwen2.5-32B base, surpassing DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B's 47 points, using only half the training steps; simultaneously, it open-sourced the training code verl, the dataset DAPO-Math-17k, and the model weights. The value of this breakdown lies in the fact that "all four mechanisms are embedded outside of GRPO," proving that the next wave of progress after R1 is not about new algorithms, but about precise attribution of GRPO failure modes and item-by-item fixes. This is a textbook example of an engineering post-mortem paper, particularly important for those attempting to reproduce R1 themselves. ## 2. Main Text Skeleton: Only One Section Discusses the Method | Section | Responsibility | Key Breakdown Points | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 Introduction | Establishing the Argument | "Key training details in the R1/Z1 report were omitted" establishes the argument; naive GRPO achieved only 30 points on 32B, showing a clear gap with the publicly reported 47 points of DeepSeek-R1 | | 2 Preliminary | Background | Core formulas for 2.1 PPO and 2.2 GRPO are clarified in just one paragraph each, avoiding confusion with the main text's methods | | 3 DAPO Algorithm | Main Method | The four mechanisms are presented in order of dependency (detailed in the next section) | | 4 Experiments | Main Experiments | Table 1 is a progressive ablation study; AIME 24/25/LLM 20 each have their own main table | | 5 Discussion | Discussion | Failure modes and potential improvement directions for each of the four mechanisms | | 6 Conclusions | Conclusion | Within one page | The main text consists of only six sections, with all reproducible engineering details (training details, baseline comparisons, reward design, prompt templates, hardware configurations) moved to Appendix A. The core asset of the methodology paper is 'mechanism attribution + ablation evidence', while all verification content is deferred to the back. ## III. Dependency Order of the Four Mechanisms Section 3 presents the four mechanisms, which the authors arrange in strict order in the formulas and main text as: 'first entropy collapse reduction, then gradient noise suppression, then response length control, then stable truncation reward': | Mechanism | Target Object | Key Design | | --- | --- | --- | | Clip-Higher | Symmetric clipping interval in PPO/GRPO | Changed to asymmetric `[1-ε_low, 1+ε_high]`, taking `ε_low = 0.2`, `ε_high = 0.28` (Equation 10) | | Dynamic Sampling | Prompt granularity | After oversampling, discard prompts with accuracy equal to 0 and 1, ensuring all prompts in the batch contribute valid gradients | | Token-Level Policy Gradient Loss | Loss normalization granularity | Change GRPO's 'first average within sequence tokens, then average across samples' to directly normalize by the total number of tokens within the group (Equation 12) | | Overlong Reward Shaping | Overly long truncated samples | Overlong Filtering shields the loss of truncated samples + Soft Overlong Punishment applies length penalty; `L_max = 16,384`, `L_cache = 4,096`, maximum generation length 20,480 (Equation 13) | Clip-Higher is the foundation, first raising entropy to create exploration space; Dynamic Sampling can truly select effective prompts only after entropy stabilizes; Token-Level Loss addresses the problem of gradient dilution in long sequences; Overlong Reward Shaping handles the reward noise that 'reasonable reasoning that was truncated should not be penalized'. Each of the four mechanisms corresponds to a specific failure mode of GRPO in long CoT training, and missing any one will cause visible degradation in the training curve. The details of selecting asymmetric intervals are also worth noting: the author deliberately avoids increasing `ε_low`, because once the lower bound is expanded, the probability of exploring low-probability tokens is pushed toward zero, triggering "sampling space collapse." The directionality of Clip-Higher is "explore more broadly upward, remain cautious downward," which is an counter-intuitive yet well-explained design. ## IV. Ablation is Additive, Not Substitutive Table 1 is the most worth-reading table in this paper, as it presents the contributions of four mechanisms in an additive manner (with substitutive ablation provided for reference): | Configuration | AIME 2024 (avg@32) | Increment | | --- | --- | --- | | DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B | 47 | External Reference | | Naive GRPO | 30 | Baseline | | + Overlong Filtering | 36 | +6 | | + Clip-Higher | 38 | +2 | | + Soft Overlong Punishment | 41 | +3 | | + Token-level Loss | 42 | +1 | | + Dynamic Sampling (full DAPO) | 50 | +8 | Dynamic Sampling alone accounts for 8 points; the authors explain that "after entropy is raised, prompts previously sacrificed can now produce effective gradients." Token-Level Loss contributes only 1 point, but in exchange for training stability and healthier growth in response length, it serves as an "indispensable engineering safeguard despite its low score." This kind of additive table, which stacks all scores onto the final item, reflects the honesty of engineering retrospection better than negative ablations that write "how many points are lost by removing this item": every mechanism has contributed, and none can be omitted. ## V. Appendix and Open-source Delivery | Resource | Location | | --- | --- | | Training Code | github.com/volcengine/verl (the verl framework itself) + BytedTsinghua-SIA/DAPO (recipe repository) | | Dataset | DAPO-Math-17k (HuggingFace) | | Model Weights | DAPO-Qwen-32B (HuggingFace) | | Project Page | dapo-sia.github.io | | Paper | arXiv:2503.14476 | The article places all engineering parameters in Appendix A: training hardware (H800 cluster × 8 cards for rollouts / 8 cards for actor), reward design (rule-based correctness + length penalty), prompt templates, and checkpoint frequency. This boundary design of 'persuasion in the main text, fulfillment in the appendix' follows the same writing tradition as Search-R1. ## 6. Three Writing Techniques Worth Learning 1. **Organize the methods section using a 'failure mode checklist'**: The authors list four specific failures in the Introduction (entropy collapse, reward noise, training instability, length loss of control), and each mechanism in Section 3 corresponds exactly to one failure. This builds a stronger intuition for readers regarding the 'necessity of mechanisms' than simply stating 'we designed four improvements'. 2. **Accumulative ablation is more powerful than replacement ablation**: Replacement ablation (dropping X results in a few points lost) can only falsify, while accumulative ablation (adding X gains points) can both falsify and verify. The design of Table 1 represents the pinnacle of engineering review papers. 3. **Second-order explanation of 'asymmetric pruning directionality'**: The authors not only provide the numerical values for `ε_high > ε_low` but also give a second-order reason for 'why not amplify the lower bound'. Readers can adopt this design without needing to re-perform counter-intuitive post-hoc attribution. ## Footnote: Mapping to My Own Work When performing LoRA fine-tuning on OKC-SFT, we also encounter degenerate batches where 'all samples are correct' or 'all samples are incorrect'. In industrial data, this type of failure mode is named 'entropy collapse' in Qwen2.5-32B RL training, and 'homogeneous batch' in the OKC-SFT 858 QA dataset. The mechanisms differ, and the names differ, but the causal chain of 'sample space collapse → gradient noise amplification' is consistent. An unexpected takeaway from reading DAPO is that mapping engineering experience from elsewhere to one's own work is more valuable than directly copying formulas. ## References - Paper: arXiv:2503.14476 v2 (2025-05-20), authors Qiying Yu et al. - Code: github.com/volcengine/verl; recipe repository github.com/BytedTsinghua-SIA/DAPO - Dataset: huggingface.co/datasets/BytedTsinghua-SIA/DAPO-Math-17k - Model weights: huggingface.co/BytedTsinghua-SIA/DAPO-Qwen-32B - Project page: dapo-sia.github.io - Main experiment protocol: For AIME 2024 evaluation, report avg@32 by sampling each problem 32 times; inference temperature = 1.0, top-p = 0.7 - Related reading: SAO (arXiv:2607.07508, structural failure and repair of GRPO group sampling in asynchronous scenarios); our breakdown is available at 'SAO Breakdown: When GRPO’s Group Sampling Collides with Asynchronous Agent Training, How to Recover After 160 Steps of Collapse'
